task: This is a synthetic newspaper-writing exercise using fictional reporting notes. Use only the supplied reporting notes. Write from the reporting snapshot as of August 31, 2026. Write a headline and a 450–650-word AP-style newspaper explainer about package-size changes at the grocery shelf, using the Marshglen cereal change to answer what an unchanged package price does and does not tell shoppers.

facts.text: Marshglen Foods began shipping a 400-gram bag of its Orchard Grain cereal in July 2026, replacing a 500-gram bag.
Both sizes sold for $4 at the three participating stores in the supplied August shelf check.
At those prices, the old bag cost $8 per kilogram and the new bag costs $10 per kilogram, a 25% increase in unit price.
The package contains 20% less cereal; that percentage differs from the 25% rise in the price per kilogram.
The new weight is printed on the front label, and the bag's shape and main color remain similar to the previous packaging.
The manufacturer says the ingredient recipe is unchanged, but the reporting record contains no independent laboratory comparison.
Company purchasing director Lora Dain says its contracted grain and dried-fruit costs increased during the past year.
The company has not disclosed a complete product-cost breakdown or the margin earned on either bag size.
Dain said, "We chose a smaller pack at the familiar ticket price rather than a larger jump on the shelf label."
The Household Basket Observatory examined ten selected packaged products for its local comparison: three became smaller, five stayed the same size and two became larger.
The observatory selected those products after shopper inquiries and does not describe them as a representative inflation sample.
Old and new cereal bags were both still on sale during the shelf check, so shoppers could encounter two unit prices at one package price.
Store manager Omi Venn said staff had replaced unit-price labels for the new stock but were keeping separate labels where both sizes remained.
Customer Rella Pike normally buys the cereal by the number of breakfasts it supplies rather than by package count.
Pike said, "Four dollars looks familiar until the bag runs out a day earlier."
Pike's experience does not establish a standardized serving size or the same number of breakfasts for every household.
The stores sometimes offer temporary multi-buy discounts, which were not running during the supplied comparison.
A lower promotional package price can change the unit-price comparison, so the observatory records price and quantity together.
Marshglen has sold the cereal under the same product name since 2017.
The packet contains no finding of misleading-label violations or evidence that every manufacturer is reducing package size.

forbidden_additions: The 20% quantity reduction equals a 20% unit-price increase
A representative national inflation measure, proven margin increase or labeling-law violation

Package price, package quantity and unit price answer different questions.
